types.javadoc:
What kind of problem a dataset describes.

This is the axis the whole model layer is organised around: a {@link Solver} declares the task it can solve, a {@link Dataset} declares the task it poses, and screening only pairs the two when they match. Adding a new family means adding a constant here and a solver that reports it — no existing solver has to change.

types.javadoc:
One dataset, in the shape its {@link Task} expects.

Two forms exist: a feature matrix with one target per row, and a token stream. Keeping both in one type is what lets {@link basalt.auto.Auto} screen classical estimators and sequence models with the same call — the dataset knows its task, and only solvers that declare the same task are considered.

Instances are immutable views: the tabular factories keep the caller's {@link Matrix} by reference (copying a large matrix on every screening run would be wasteful), the sequence factory copies the id array because it is small and often built inline.

types.javadoc:
A trained model, whatever family it came from.

Two capabilities, and a model only has the ones its task needs: tabular models predict one value per row, sequence models generate a continuation as token ids — mapping ids to glyphs is the caller's business, because the library never assumes a charset. The unused one throws {@link UnsupportedOperationException} with a message that says which kind of model you are holding, so a mistake surfaces immediately instead of returning garbage.

types.javadoc:
One trainable candidate: a named recipe that can score itself on a dataset and then be fitted on all of it.

This is the seam that lets one screening loop compare a decision forest with a neural network and a character-level language model. A solver is a stateless descriptor — it holds configuration, not weights — so the same instance can be scored and fitted any number of times.

Two contracts matter:

  • {@link #score} must return a number where larger is better, computed without touching the rows it reports on. Classical solvers cross-validate; neural solvers hold out a slice and train once, because a full k-fold sweep of a network is far more expensive than the model it is ranking.
  • {@link #fit} trains on everything and returns something that can predict or generate.

一个可训练的候选：能给自己打分，也能在全部数据上拟合
body: 这就是让同一个筛选循环可以比较决策森林、神经网络和字符级语言模型的接缝。Solver 是无状态的描述符——只持有配置，不持有权重——所以同一个实例可以被反复打分和拟合。
两条约定：score 必须返回越大越好的数字，并且不能偷看它报告的那些行；分类/回归走交叉验证，神经网络留出一片数据训一次，因为对网络做完整 k 折的开销远高于它要排序的模型本身。fit 用全部数据训练，返回可预测或可生成的对象。

types.javadoc:
Adapts a registered {@link Estimator} to the {@link Solver} contract.

Scoring uses k-fold cross-validation — these models are cheap enough that a full sweep costs nothing next to a single epoch of a network, and cross-validation is far less noisy than one holdout split when the dataset is small.

types.javadoc:
A neural candidate: an architecture plus the training recipe that turns it into a model.

Two shapes are supported, matching the two data forms. Tabular candidates read raw feature columns and emit one class or one value per row; sequence candidates read a window of token ids and emit a distribution over the next one.

Scoring holds out a slice and trains once, where {@link ClassicalSolver} cross-validates. The asymmetry is deliberate: a five-fold sweep of a network costs five trainings, and for the purpose of ranking candidates a single honest holdout is enough. The price is a noisier estimate on very small datasets, which is why the screening table reports the numbers rather than hiding them.

body: 支持两种形状，对应两种数据形态。表格候选读原始特征列，每行输出一个类别或一个值；序列候选读一个 token 窗口，输出下一个 token 的分布。

types.javadoc:
Catalogue of everything that can be screened, across every model family.

Classical solvers are derived, not copied: every supervised algorithm in {@link Registry} appears here as a {@link ClassicalSolver}, built on demand. That keeps the two extension points connected — registering an {@link basalt.ml.Estimator} with {@code Registry} is enough for it to be screened, without also having to wrap it. Solvers that are not classical (networks, language models) have no estimator behind them, so they are registered explicitly.

Names are case-insensitive and may only be used once; replacing silently would make a screening report impossible to reproduce.
